newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jobless dip gives French government poll boost.
newsitem.headline: Jobless dip gives French government poll boost.

text.p: France's centre-right government got a campaign boost on Wednesday when the last unemployment figures to be released before a parliamentary election next month showed a slight dip in the giant jobless total.

Unemployment fell by 4,800 to 3,087,500 in March, according to national criteria, although the jobless rate calculated on International Labour Organisation (ILO) rules remained at the record 12.8 percent of the workforce it reached in February.
Jumping the gun on the official statistics, Prime Minister Alain Juppe boasted on Tuesday that the second consecutive monthly fall in March showed "the rise in unemployment has been stopped".
His campaign-tinted optimism contrasted with a forecast by the International Monetary Fund last week that France's jobless rate would continue to rise to more than 13 percent this year.
Opinion polls show unemployment is the number one voter concern and its continued rise under Juppe's government is one of the main causes of his unpopularity.
Economists said the figures were politically convenient and pointed to the discrepancy between the domestic and ILO figures.

"In an electoral campaign environment these figures have to be taken with a pinch of salt. It looks like unemployment data is not meant to interfere with the campaign," said JP Morgan economist David Naude. "Needless to say in the current environment these figures are of little informative value."
Opposition Socialist parliamentary floor leader Laurent Fabius accused Juppe on Tuesday night of manipulating the figures to try to conceal the real level of unemployment.
"The reality is that unemployment is closer to five million than three million," Fabius told a campaign rally in the prime minister's adopted hometown of Bordeaux.

And conservative National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, distancing himself from fellow Gaullist Juppe's platform, said the fight against unemployment should be at the heart of the election campaign and of government policy.
The next monthly figures are not due to be published until June 2, a day after the election runoff.
French unemployment is the highest in the Group of Seven major industrial democracies, although the country has a forest of job-creation subsidies and work experience programmes.
Conservative economists blame the record on an over-rigid labour market, a high minimum wage and payroll social charges and bureaucratic regulation of business.

Left-wing economists point to a cycle of stagnant purchasing power, anaemic consumer demand and low investment, and some blame the deficit-cutting austerity imposed by Juppe to meet the criteria for a single European currency.
Left and right have set out sharply different approaches to creating jobs in their election platforms.

The centre-right coalition has stressed curbing public spending, cutting payroll charges on the low paid, negotiating more flexible working hours and slimming down the civil service to promote employment in the private sector.

The Socialist and Communist parties pledged on Tuesday to create 700,000 jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector, legislate to reduce the work week gradually to 35 hours from 39 and measures to boost wages and consumer demand.
